text_blocks.snippet: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is transmitted through specific bodily fluids and certain risky behaviors. The primary ways HIV is spread are through unprotected anal or vaginal sex, sharing needles or other drug injection equipment, and from a mother to her child during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding. It is not transmitted through casual contact like hugging, shaking hands, or sharing utensils.
snippet_highlighted_words: through unprotected anal or vaginal sex, sharing needles or other drug injection equipment, and from a mother to her child during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding

list.title: Unprotected sex:
list.snippet: HIV can be transmitted through vaginal or anal sex when a condom is not used or is used incorrectly, as semen, pre-seminal fluid, vaginal fluids, and rectal fluids can carry the virus.

list.title: Oral sex:
list.snippet: While the risk is lower than anal or vaginal sex, oral sex can also transmit HIV, particularly if there are open sores or bleeding in the mouth or genitals.

list.title: Injection drug use:
list.snippet: Sharing needles, syringes, or other drug injection equipment with someone who has HIV can directly inject the virus into your bloodstream.

list.title: Other equipment:
list.snippet: Sharing equipment used for tattooing or piercing can also pose a risk if it's not properly sterilized.
During pregnancy: HIV can be transmitted from a pregnant person with HIV to their baby through the placenta.
During birth: Transmission can also occur during delivery as the baby passes through the birth canal.
Breastfeeding: HIV can be transmitted through breast milk.

list.title: Blood transfusions:
list.snippet: While rare in countries with proper blood screening, HIV can be transmitted through blood transfusions if the blood is contaminated.

list.title: Accidental needle sticks:
list.snippet: Healthcare workers and others can be exposed to HIV through accidental needle sticks with contaminated blood.

list.title: Other body fluids:
list.snippet: Exposure to HIV-infected blood, semen, vaginal fluids, or breast milk through open wounds or mucous membranes can also transmit the virus.
HIV is not transmitted through casual contact, such as hugging, shaking hands, or sharing food.
HIV is not transmitted through saliva, sweat, or urine.
There are effective ways to prevent HIV transmission, including PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis), PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis), and consistent condom use.
People with HIV who take antiretroviral therapy (ART) and have an undetectable viral load cannot transmit HIV to their sexual partners.

key_moments.title: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is transmitted from person to person through blood, semen, vaginal fluids and breastmilk.
HIV can enter the body through the lining of the vagina, penis, or anus during sex without a condom, through sharing injecting equipment or through breastfeeding.
Once it is in the body. HIV travels through the blood and targets key elements of the immune system called T cells.
HIV particles search and find Special receptors called CD4 receptors on the outside of the T cell
The virus then merges with the T cell and begins to insert its genetic material.
The HIV reproductive cycle has seriously damaged the T cell, which will now die.
